0.title: The Verdict That Changes Everything
0.essay:
Every human being lives before a court. We may never use the word, but we feel it: the sense that our lives are being weighed, that someone is keeping score, that a verdict is coming. The Bible says the feeling is true. There is a Judge, and his verdict is the one that lasts.

The best news in the world

The Christian gospel is not first of all advice about how to live. It is an announcement about a verdict. God, the Judge of all the earth, declares guilty people righteous in his sight, not because they have become good enough, but because of what Jesus Christ has done for them, and he does it for everyone who simply trusts in Christ. That is what the Bible calls justification, and the Reformers called it the article on which the church stands or falls.

It answers the oldest question a conscience can ask: how can I be right with God? And it answers it in a way no human religion would ever have invented. God does not lower the standard, and he does not pretend we have met it. He meets it himself, in his Son, and then counts that Son’s perfect record as ours.

What this study does

The study The Doctrines of Grace has a chapter that sets out the doctrine in outline. This study goes more slowly, text by text. We will ask what the word “justify” really means, how God can be just when he acquits the guilty, what it means for Christ’s righteousness to be counted to us, why faith and faith alone receives it, and how Abraham and David knew this gospel long before Paul wrote it down. We will read James 2 carefully, listen fairly to Christians who see things differently, and end with the peace that the verdict brings.

Several studies sit close by. Union with Christ shows how every blessing, justification included, is ours in him. Assurance of Salvation explores how a believer can know he is accepted. The Grace of God, Good Works and The Three Uses of the Law fill out the picture.

The chapters

The Question of All Questions; Declared Righteous: What “Justify” Means; The Great Exchange; Faith Alone: The Empty Hand; Abraham and David: The Gospel Before the Gospel; Paul and James: Faith Alone, but Never Alone; Where Christians Differ; and Peace with God.

For reflection

Whose verdict on your life do you most care about at the moment? If God asked you today why he should accept you, what would you honestly say?

1.title: The Question of All Questions
1.essay:
Somewhere in the middle of his suffering, with his friends lecturing him and his body covered in sores, Job asks a question that goes deeper than any of theirs. It is not “Why am I suffering?” It is this: “But how can a man be in the right before God?” (Job 9:2).

An old question

Job is no fool. He knows God is wise and mighty, and he knows what it would mean to stand in God’s court and argue his case: “If one wished to contend with him, one could not answer him once in a thousand times” (Job 9:3). Later his friend Bildad asks the same thing in almost the same words: “How then can man be in the right before God? How can he who is born of woman be pure?” (Job 25:4). Neither of them has an answer. Job can only long for someone who does not yet exist: “There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both” (Job 9:33).

That is the question of all questions. Not “Is there a God?”, important as that is, but “If there is, where do I stand with him?” Every religion is, in one way or another, an attempt to answer it.

We are all lawyers

Modern people rarely use courtroom language about God, yet we have not stopped living in a courtroom. We justify ourselves all day long. We explain why we were late, why the remark was not really unkind, why our anger was reasonable. We scroll through other people’s lives and quietly weigh our own. We want to be told we are good parents, good at our jobs, good people. Underneath all of it is a hunger for a verdict: you are acceptable; you are enough.

The Gospels show the instinct with painful honesty. A lawyer asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life, answers his own question correctly, and is told, “do this, and you will live.” Then Luke adds: “But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, ‘And who is my neighbor?’” (Luke 10:28–29). He wanted the law small enough to keep. So do we. We move the line until we are on the right side of it.

Every mouth stopped

Paul refuses to let anyone move the line. In Romans 1 to 3 he calls the whole human race into court, first the openly wicked, then the morally respectable, then the religious. His summary is devastating: “None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God” (Romans 3:10–11). Then comes the point of it all: “Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God” (Romans 3:19).

Every mouth stopped. In an earthly court the defendant at least has something to say. Here the defence has nothing left. And the reason is stated plainly: “For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20). The law is a mirror, not a ladder. It shows us what we are; it cannot lift us to where we should be. The studies The Three Uses of the Law and The Truth About Sin explore this further.

A monk who could not find peace

Few people have felt the weight of this question more than Martin Luther. In 1505, as a young law student caught in a violent thunderstorm, he vowed to become a monk, and he kept the vow, entering the Augustinian house at Erfurt. He threw himself into the life: fasting, long prayers, sleepless vigils and confessions so thorough they could last for hours. He later said that if anyone could have reached heaven by monkery, he would have been that monk. Yet none of it brought peace. The more seriously he took God, the more clearly he saw that his heart was not right. His question, as it is often summed up, was how he could find a gracious God.

His superior, Johann von Staupitz, set him to teach the Bible at the new university in Wittenberg. Lecturing through the Psalms and then Romans, Luther wrestled with the phrase “the righteousness of God” in Romans 1:17. He had taken it to mean the righteousness by which God judges and punishes sinners, and, as he admitted near the end of his life, he had come to hate it. Then he saw that Paul meant the righteousness God gives, freely, to those who believe. The study The Doctrines of Grace gives his own account of that discovery. Historians still debate exactly when it happened. What it did is not in doubt: it opened the door of the Reformation.

Why it is still the question

A retired teacher, kind and widely respected, sat with her minister after a friend’s funeral. She said she had always assumed God marked on a curve, and that she would pass comfortably. Then, at the graveside, it struck her that she had no idea where the pass mark was, or who had set it. She had spent her life being decent. She had never asked whether decent was the same as righteous.

Her question was Job’s question, and Luther’s, and ours. The psalmist puts it in one breath with its answer: “If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (Psalm 130:3–4). No one could stand. And yet there is forgiveness. How both can be true, how a holy Judge can welcome the guilty without becoming unjust, is what the rest of this study is about. The answer, when it comes, will not be a theory. It will be a Person: the very arbiter Job longed for, who lays his hand on God and on us both.

For reflection

Where do you notice yourself “justifying yourself” in everyday life? Why does Paul insist that “every mouth” must be stopped before the good news can be heard? Have you ever, like the retired teacher, assumed God marks on a curve? What does Job’s longing for an “arbiter” stir in you?

2.title: Declared Righteous: What “Justify” Means
2.essay:
Words matter, and few words matter more than this one. Everything in the doctrine of justification depends on what the Bible means when it says that God “justifies” someone. Does he make a person good, or declare a person to be in the right? The answer changes the whole shape of the Christian life.

A word from the courtroom

The Old Testament uses the word in the setting of a law court. Moses instructs Israel’s judges: “If there is a dispute between men and they come into court and the judges decide between them, acquitting the innocent and condemning the guilty” (Deuteronomy 25:1). Where the ESV says “acquitting the innocent”, the Hebrew says, literally, “justifying the righteous”. A judge does not make anyone innocent. He cannot reach into the defendant’s heart and change it. He weighs the evidence and pronounces a verdict. To justify is to declare a person to be in the right before the law.

Proverbs makes the point sharper still: “He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD” (Proverbs 17:15). If “justify” meant “make righteous”, then justifying the wicked would be a beautiful thing, the transformation of bad people into good ones. It is an abomination only because it means declaring the guilty innocent. That is what corrupt judges do when they take a bribe.

The same word everywhere

The New Testament uses the word the same way. When the crowds heard Jesus speak about John the Baptist, Luke says, “they declared God just” (Luke 7:29): in Greek, they “justified God”. Nobody makes God righteous. They acknowledged that he was. And Jesus warns that on the last day, “by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matthew 12:37). The opposite of “justify” is not “corrupt” but “condemn”.

Paul’s great courtroom scene settles it: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn?” (Romans 8:33–34). Justification is the verdict of acquittal, the opposite of the sentence of condemnation.

A verdict, not a process

This is why justification is complete the moment it is given. Jesus told of two men who went up to the temple to pray, a Pharisee and a tax collector. One listed his achievements. The other stood far off and beat his breast, “saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’” And Jesus said, “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other” (Luke 18:13–14). He went down justified that same afternoon. He was not partly justified, or justified on probation, or justified as long as he kept improving. He walked home in the right with God.

God does also change the people he justifies. He gives them a new heart and makes them holy, slowly and truly, for the rest of their lives. But that is a different gift, which the Bible calls sanctification. Sanctification grows; justification does not. A believer who has walked with Christ for fifty years is no more justified than the thief who trusted him on the cross that afternoon. He is, we hope, more holy. He is not more accepted. The studies Union with Christ and Fighting Sin & Temptation show how the two belong together without ever being confused.

The scandal of Romans 4:5

Now read this slowly. Paul says the believer trusts “in him who justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5). Not the godly. Not those who are trying hard. The ungodly. Set that beside Proverbs 17:15. God forbids human judges to do the very thing he says he does himself. If God simply waved guilt away, he would be the corrupt judge of Proverbs, and the moral universe would be a lie. The Bible is not naive about this. It knows that a God who forgives cheaply is not good.

Just and the justifier

So how can it be? Paul answers in the densest paragraph he ever wrote. “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law” (Romans 3:21). Sinners “are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith” (Romans 3:24–25). A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger, and the Greek word is the one used for the mercy seat, the lid of the ark where the blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement.

Paul then explains why it had to be so. For centuries God had “passed over former sins” (Romans 3:25). He had forgiven Abraham, Moses, David and countless others, and had not yet punished their sins. It might have looked as if he did not care. At the cross he showed otherwise. “It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

Just, and the justifier. God does not choose between his justice and his mercy. He does not lower the bar, or bend the law, or pretend. The sentence is carried out in full, and it falls on his own Son, who goes willingly. The Judge’s justice is not set aside; it is satisfied. And so the verdict “righteous” over a guilty sinner is not a bribe or a blind eye. It is the most just verdict ever spoken, because the debt has been paid.

A young man said he had always thought of the Christian life as permanent probation: one false move and the sentence would be reinstated. Reading Romans 3 with an older friend, he saw for the first time that the case had not been adjourned. It had been closed, and closed justly. He did not stop taking sin seriously. He started taking the cross seriously, and found that the two went together.

For reflection

Why does it matter so much that “justify” means to declare, not to make? Why would Proverbs 17:15 make Romans 4:5 so startling to a first-century Jewish reader? How does the cross allow God to be both “just and the justifier”? Do you tend to think of your standing with God as a closed case or as permanent probation?

3.title: The Great Exchange
3.essay:
A just judge does not declare a person righteous without a reason. If God declares the ungodly righteous, there must be a righteousness on which the verdict rests. The Bible’s answer: the righteousness is real, it is perfect, and it belongs to someone else.

A word from the account book

In Romans 4 Paul uses one word again and again: “counted”. “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Romans 4:3). It is a bookkeeping word, the word for entering something in a ledger and putting it to someone’s account. Theologians call it imputation.

Paul shows that the ledger has two columns. On one side, sin is not counted. He quotes David: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin” (Romans 4:7–8). On the other side, righteousness is counted. David speaks “of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works” (Romans 4:6). Our debts are cancelled, and a credit is entered that we never earned.

More than a clean slate

Why both? Would forgiveness not be enough? Forgiveness alone would leave us with a blank page. But God’s law does not merely forbid evil. It commands love: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37) and “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:39). To stand before God we need not only the absence of guilt but the presence of a life of perfect love. We have never lived one. Christ has.

Paul sets the two heads of humanity side by side: “For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). Not by our obedience, but by his.

His whole obedience

What did that obedience include? Reformed Christians answer: all of it. The Son of God was “born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). At his baptism he said, “thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15). For some thirty years he loved his Father with all his heart and his neighbour as himself, in every hour, in every thought, through every temptation. Then “he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8). Theologians call the first his active obedience, his keeping of the law, and the second his passive obedience, his suffering of its penalty. Both are counted to the believer. The 1689 Baptist Confession, following the Savoy Declaration of 1658, says God justifies by imputing Christ’s “active obedience unto the whole Law, and passive obedience in his death, for their whole and sole Righteousness”. The Heidelberg Catechism puts it in the first person: God treats me “as if I had never committed nor had any sin, and had myself accomplished all the obedience which Christ has fulfilled for me” (Question 60).

Not every Christian who holds to justification by faith puts it this way. Some, from the German theologian Johannes Piscator around 1600 to scholars today, hold that only Christ’s death is counted to us. They too rest on Christ alone, and that should be honoured. But the Reformed reading does better justice to Romans 5:19, to Paul’s longing for “the righteousness from God” (Philippians 3:9), and to the prophecy that the coming King will be called “The LORD is our righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:6). Our righteousness is not a thing. It is a Person, and the whole of his life is ours.

He made him to be sin

The exchange is stated most boldly in one verse: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Christ did not become sinful. He was counted as the sinner, and treated so. We do not become sinless in ourselves. We are counted righteous, and treated so. The little words “in him” explain how this is just: joined to Christ by faith, we share what is his, as the study Union with Christ explains.

Paul had an impressive record of his own: “circumcised on the eighth day … as to the law, a Pharisee … as to righteousness under the law, blameless” (Philippians 3:5–6). He threw it all away, not just his worst deeds but his best, “in order that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ” (Philippians 3:8–9). Found in him: on the last day, that is the only place to be found.

Filthy garments and a clean turban

Long before Paul, God gave his people a picture. In a vision the prophet Zechariah saw Joshua the high priest “standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him” (Zechariah 3:1). Joshua was “clothed with filthy garments” (Zechariah 3:3). The accuser had a case. Joshua says nothing at all; he has no defence. Then the angel of the LORD, whom this commentary takes to be the Son of God before his coming in the flesh, gives the command: “Remove the filthy garments from him.” And to Joshua he says, “Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments” (Zechariah 3:4). Something is taken away, and something is put on.

Isaiah sings the same song: “he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10). Count Zinzendorf’s hymn, in John Wesley’s translation, says it simply: “Jesus, thy blood and righteousness / My beauty are, my glorious dress.”

A man came to faith while serving a prison sentence. Years later he told his home group what had undone him. He had expected, at best, that God would wipe his record. He had not expected God to hand him a different file altogether, with another man’s name on the cover and his own written underneath. “I walked in with my record,” he said, “and walked out with his.”

For reflection

Why is forgiveness alone not the whole of what we need before God? What difference does it make to you that Christ’s whole life, and not only his death, was lived for you? Which of your “best deeds” are you tempted to wear before God instead of Christ’s robe? How does Zechariah 3 speak to you when your conscience accuses you?

4.title: Faith Alone: The Empty Hand
4.essay:
If our righteousness is Christ’s, how does it become ours? The Bible’s answer is always the same: through faith. But that answer can be misunderstood in two opposite ways, and both are deadly. Faith can be treated as too little, or it can be made into too much.

Why faith, and only faith?

Paul says it without qualification: “For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:28). And again: “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9). The Reformers added the word “alone” not to improve on Paul but to say what he meant. If anything else were added, it would not be “apart from works” any longer.

Paul also explains why God chose faith. “That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring” (Romans 4:16). Faith fits grace as a hand fits a glove. Of all the things a human being can do, believing is the one thing that adds nothing. It does not pay; it receives. It does not build; it rests. And because it adds nothing, the promise can be “guaranteed”. If the promise depended even slightly on our performance, it would be guaranteed to no one.

That is why Paul is so fierce with the Galatians, who had trusted Christ but were being told they must also be circumcised. “You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace” (Galatians 5:4). A bridge that reaches ninety-nine per cent of the way across a gorge is not nearly a bridge. Christ plus anything is not a better Christ. It is another gospel.

Faith is not a work

The opposite danger is subtler. Some Christians quietly turn faith into the new good work. They are not trusting their giving or their churchgoing any longer; now they are trusting the quality of their believing. Did I believe sincerely enough? Was my repentance deep enough? Did I really mean the prayer? Faith becomes one more performance to be anxiously checked.

The confessions of the Reformation saw this coming. The Westminster Confession says God justifies sinners “not by imputing faith itself, the act of believing, or any other evangelical obedience to them, as their righteousness” (11.1), and calls faith “the alone instrument of justification” (11.2). An instrument is a tool. The Heidelberg Catechism asks why I am righteous only by faith, and answers: “Not that I am acceptable to God on account of the worthiness of my faith” (Question 61), but because Christ’s righteousness is mine, and faith is the only way to receive it.

Faith, then, is an empty hand. A beggar who holds out his hand for bread is not paying for it, and nobody praises him for the strength of his fingers. Faith does include knowing the truth about Christ and agreeing that it is true. “Even the demons believe” that much (James 2:19). But at its heart it is trust: as the Confession puts it, “receiving and resting on Christ and his righteousness” (11.2). It is the soul leaning its whole weight on him.

The strength is in the object

When the Israelites in the wilderness were dying from snakebite, God told Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole: “And if a serpent bit anyone, he would look at the bronze serpent and live” (Numbers 21:9). Some of those who looked must have been half blind with fever. Some must have looked with doubt, some with desperate hope, some barely lifting their heads. All who looked lived, because the healing was not in their eyes but on the pole. Jesus took that story for himself: “as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15).

A person who crawls trembling across thick ice is perfectly safe. A person who strides confidently across thin ice goes through it. What holds you up is not the strength of your confidence but the strength of what you are standing on. So the father who cried, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24) went home with his son healed. The woman who crept up behind Jesus and touched the fringe of his garment, half afraid, perhaps half superstitious, heard him say, “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well” (Matthew 9:22). Weak faith in a strong Saviour justifies as surely as strong faith, because it lays hold of the same Christ. Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s famous advice is still the best: for every look at yourself, take ten looks at Christ.

A warmed heart

On 24 May 1738 John Wesley, an Anglican clergyman who had been a missionary in Georgia and had lived a life of strict devotion for years, went reluctantly to a meeting in Aldersgate Street in London. Someone was reading Luther’s preface to the letter to the Romans. Wesley wrote in his journal that he felt his heart “strangely warmed”, and that he did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation. He had been religious for years. That evening he stopped leaning on his religion and leaned on Christ.

A teenage boy had “asked Jesus into his heart” dozens of times, each time afraid that he had not done it properly. His youth leader asked him what the Israelites in the wilderness were told to look at. “The serpent on the pole,” he said. “Not at their own eyes?” He laughed, and something in him relaxed. If anxious checking of this kind ever becomes constant and tormenting, it is worth talking with a pastor or a biblical counsellor, who will usually also suggest a medical check-up. God’s Word is sufficient for the soul, and seeking medical help is no failure of faith.

For reflection

Why does faith, more than any other response, fit with grace? Have you ever made your faith into a performance to be checked? What does the bronze serpent teach you about weak faith? Where would looking at Christ, rather than at yourself, help you this week?

5.title: Abraham and David: The Gospel Before the Gospel
5.essay:
Is justification by faith a new idea, invented by Paul or rediscovered by Luther? Paul anticipated the question and answered it with the two greatest names in Israel’s history: Abraham, the father of the nation, and David, its greatest king.

Under the stars

Genesis 15 begins with a discouraged old man. God has promised Abram a great nation, yet he and Sarah are childless, and his heir is a servant. So God takes him outside and tells him to count the stars: “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5). There was nothing to see but the promise and the night sky. And then comes one of the most important sentences in the Bible: “And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). It is the first time in Scripture that anyone is said to believe.

Abram was not chosen because he was a saint. Joshua later reminded Israel that his family “served other gods” (Joshua 24:2). He was called out of idolatry. It is no accident that Paul, having introduced Abraham, at once speaks of God as the one “who justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5).

God alone walks between the pieces

The rest of Genesis 15 is strange to modern readers and wonderful once understood. God tells Abram to cut animals in half and lay the halves opposite each other. In the ancient world, covenant partners would sometimes walk between such pieces, as if to say: may I be torn apart like these animals if I break my word. Jeremiah refers to the custom (Jeremiah 34:18). But Abram does not walk between them. He falls into a deep sleep. Then “a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces” (Genesis 15:17), a sign of God’s own presence. God alone walks the path. God alone takes the oath, and the curse that goes with it.

The faith that was counted as righteousness was not Abram’s contribution to a partnership. It was a sleeping man’s trust in a God who bound himself. And centuries later, the God who walked between the pieces bore the curse himself: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

As good as dead

Paul draws out what kind of faith this was. Abraham trusted the God “who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Romans 4:17). Faith did not pretend. “He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah’s womb” (Romans 4:19). He looked hard at the facts, and then looked harder at God.

Then Paul turns to us: “But the words ‘it was counted to him’ were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:23–25). Our faith has the same shape as Abraham’s: trust in the God who brings life out of death. And there is a depth here worth pausing over. Christ was delivered up because of our sins; he was raised because the payment was complete. The resurrection was the Father’s verdict on his Son. Paul elsewhere says Christ was “vindicated by the Spirit” (1 Timothy 3:16), and the Greek word is the word “justified”. The empty tomb is God’s public declaration that the Son is righteous and his work accepted. When we are joined to him, his verdict becomes ours.

David, who had no works to offer

Abraham might seem a respectable example, a man of faith with a long and faithful life. So Paul adds a second witness of a very different kind. “David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works” (Romans 4:6), and Paul quotes Psalm 32: “Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity” (Psalm 32:1–2).

David knew what he was talking about. He had taken Bathsheba, arranged her husband’s death and covered it up. Many readers connect Psalm 32 with that dark chapter, as Psalm 51 certainly is. He describes the misery of hiding: “For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3). Then he confessed, “and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:5). When he admitted his sin to Nathan, the answer came at once: “The LORD also has put away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13).

Abraham shows that justification comes before any good works. David shows that it comes in spite of terrible ones. One was an honoured patriarch, the other an adulterer and murderer. Both stood on exactly the same ground: God counted righteousness to them apart from works.

The gospel preached beforehand

Paul makes the same argument to the Galatians, and adds a remarkable phrase: “the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, ‘In you shall all the nations be blessed’” (Galatians 3:8). The gospel did not begin in the first century. There has only ever been one way to be right with God. Old Testament believers looked forward, through promise and sacrifice, to the Christ who would come; we look back to the Christ who has come. The studies Covenant Theology and Christ in the Old Testament trace this one gospel through the whole Bible.

At a communion service, an old man who had been an elder for forty years sat beside a woman who had come to faith only months before, after a life she did not like to talk about. Afterwards he said to her, quietly, that they had just eaten the same bread for the same reason. She thought he was being kind. He was being exact.

For reflection

Why do you think Paul chose both Abraham and David, rather than just one of them? What does God passing alone between the pieces tell you about the covenant of grace? How does Christ’s resurrection as his “justification” encourage your faith? Which of the two, Abraham or David, do you feel closer to, and why?

6.title: Paul and James: Faith Alone, but Never Alone
6.essay:
Sooner or later every thoughtful reader of the New Testament reaches James 2:24 and stops: “You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone” (James 2:24). It is the only place in the Bible where the words “faith alone” appear, and they appear with a “not” in front of them. The honest thing is not to hurry past, but to read the whole passage slowly.

A faith that someone says he has

James begins with a question: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?” (James 2:14). Notice two small words. The first is “says”. James is examining a claim. Someone says he has faith; the question is whether what he has deserves the name. The second is “that”. James does not ask whether faith can save. He asks whether that faith can save, the kind he is about to describe. His whole argument is about what sort of faith is real.

His first picture is painfully ordinary. A brother or sister has no coat and no food, and a fellow Christian says, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” and does nothing (James 2:16). Kind words, no help. “So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead” (James 2:17). James does not call it weak faith or immature faith. He calls it dead: a corpse that still has the shape of a living thing.

Orthodox demons

Then James takes the most sacred sentence a Jew could say, the confession that God is one, and turns it into a warning. “You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and shudder!” (James 2:19). The demons are perfectly orthodox. In the Gospels they often say who Jesus is before the disciples do. They even have strong feelings about it: they tremble. Yet they are not saved. Neither correct belief nor strong feeling is the same as trust that clings to Christ. A faith that is only information, or only emotion, is the faith of devils.

Genesis 15 fulfilled in Genesis 22

Now James turns to Abraham, just as Paul does, and this is where readers think they see a contradiction. “Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar?” (James 2:21). But look at what James says next: “You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works; and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness’” (James 2:22–23).

James quotes Genesis 15:6, Paul’s own text. He does not deny that Abraham was counted righteous by faith; he takes it for granted. Then he says that Genesis 22, many years later, “fulfilled” it. That is the language of a prophecy coming true. The verdict spoken under the stars was shown to be true on the mountain. Abraham’s faith was “completed”, brought to its full expression, the way a tree is completed by its fruit.

Two meanings of one word

So James uses “justified” in a sense the Bible knows well: shown to be in the right, proved genuine. It is the sense in which Jesus said, “wisdom is justified by all her children” (Luke 7:35). Paul answers the question, On what ground does God accept a sinner? His answer: on the ground of Christ’s righteousness, received by faith apart from works. James answers a different question: What does the faith that receives Christ look like? His answer: it is alive, and life always shows. When James denies that we are justified “by faith alone”, he means by a faith that stays alone, the claimed, workless faith of verse 14. Paul would agree. He says that what counts in Christ is “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

Rahab, by faith and by works

James’s second example is Rahab, a Canaanite prostitute, about as far from Abraham as a person could be. “Was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way?” (James 2:25). Hebrews describes the very same act this way: “By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies” (Hebrews 11:31). One writer calls it works, the other calls it faith, and both are right. Her faith had already spoken: “for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath” (Joshua 2:11). Then it acted, at the risk of her life. Faith and works are not two rival roads. They are the root and the fruit of one life.

James ends with a picture: “For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead” (James 2:26). Works are like breath. Breath does not make a body alive, but a body that never breathes is not alive.

Who needs James?

Paul and James are not fighting each other. They are standing back to back, facing different enemies. Paul faces the person who thinks he can earn God’s favour. James faces the person who thinks a decision once made, or a creed once agreed to, can sit in a drawer like a ticket while his life goes on unchanged. Paul, too, has a word for him: “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!” (Romans 6:1–2).

A man in his forties had grown up in church and “made a decision” at a summer camp when he was twelve. For thirty years he had not prayed, read the Bible or cared about Christ, but he was sure he was safe: he had the date written in his Bible. A friend read James 2 with him and asked, gently, whether a living faith could stay that quiet for thirty years. It was the most loving question anyone had ever asked him.

James is medicine for the careless. The tender believer who already examines himself anxiously needs the promises first, as the study Assurance of Salvation explains; the study Good Works shows how the fruit grows.

For reflection

Why do the small words “says” and “that” in James 2:14 matter so much? How can Genesis 22 “fulfil” Genesis 15:6? What does it teach you that Hebrews calls Rahab’s act “faith” and James calls it “works”? Is there an area of your life where your faith has gone quiet?

7.title: Where Christians Differ
7.essay:
Justification divided Western Christianity in the sixteenth century, and Christians still disagree about it today. Disagreement is no excuse for caricature. This chapter sets out the two most important alternatives as their own best defenders would put them, asks what each gets right, and then explains why this commentary holds the view it does.

The Roman Catholic view

The Council of Trent issued its decree on justification in January 1547. It is a careful document, and it begins with grace. Trent taught that no one can be justified by his own works or natural powers, and that nothing that comes before justification, whether faith or works, merits the grace of justification itself.

But Trent defined justification as more than forgiveness. It is, the Council said, also the sanctification and renewal of the inner person. The righteousness by which we are justified is God’s righteousness, not in the sense of the righteousness by which God himself is righteous, but the righteousness he pours into us, so that we truly become righteous within. Because it is an inner reality, justification can increase as the justified person keeps God’s commandments with the help of grace. It can be lost by mortal sin, and it can be restored through the sacrament of penance, which Trent, borrowing an ancient image, called a second plank after shipwreck. Good works done in grace truly merit an increase of grace and eternal life, though Trent was careful to say that these merits are themselves God’s gifts. And it denied that anyone can know with the certainty of faith that he has obtained God’s grace. The Catechism of the Catholic Church of 1992 restates this teaching.

In 1999 the Lutheran World Federation and the Roman Catholic Church signed a Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, confessing together that we are accepted by God by grace alone, through faith in Christ’s saving work, not because of any merit of our own. It was a real step. But many Protestants judged that the central question, whether our inner renewal belongs to the ground of justification, was left unresolved.

What Rome rightly sees, and where it goes wrong

Catholic teaching rightly insists that grace really changes people. God does not justify anyone and then leave him as he was. Faith without love is dead, and “the holiness without which no one will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14) is not optional. Protestants who forget this have deserved Rome’s criticism.

But Scripture distinguishes what Trent combines. The tax collector “went down to his house justified” (Luke 18:14) before any renewal had had time to show. God “justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5), not the renewed. And if my justification includes my renewal, my standing with God is as unfinished as my holiness, and the “peace with God” of Romans 5:1 can never be settled. Renewal is the fruit of the verdict, never its ground.

The New Perspective on Paul

The second challenge comes from within Protestant scholarship. In 1977 E. P. Sanders published Paul and Palestinian Judaism, arguing that the Judaism of Paul’s day was not a religion of earning salvation by good deeds. He called its pattern “covenantal nomism”: Israel got in by God’s gracious choice and stayed in by obedience, with sacrifice and repentance provided for failure. James Dunn popularised the name “the New Perspective on Paul” in a lecture of 1982, and argued that “works of the law” mean above all the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles: circumcision, the food laws and the Sabbath. Paul’s target, on this reading, was not self-righteous moralism but ethnic exclusivism.

N. T. Wright argues that justification is God’s declaration of who belongs to his covenant family, Jew and Gentile together, and that “the righteousness of God” is chiefly God’s own faithfulness to his covenant promises. He questions the traditional idea of Christ’s righteousness being transferred to us, preferring to speak of believers being incorporated into the Messiah, and he speaks of a final justification on the last day in accordance with the whole life lived in the power of the Spirit. Some scholars also read Paul’s phrase “faith in Jesus Christ” as “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ”.

What the New Perspective rightly sees

There is real gold here. Christians have sometimes caricatured Judaism, and Sanders forced a needed correction. Paul’s letters are full of the unity of Jew and Gentile, and the crisis at Antioch, when Peter stopped eating with Gentile believers, was about the dinner table (Galatians 2:11–14). Justification really does have consequences for the church: you cannot be justified by faith alone and then refuse to eat with a brother whose background differs from yours. And the faithfulness of Christ is at the heart of the gospel. His obedience is the very righteousness counted to us.

But the New Perspective is not the whole of Paul. Later studies, such as the two volumes of Justification and Variegated Nomism (2001 and 2004), showed that the Judaism of the period was more varied than Sanders allowed, and that trust in one’s own obedience was not absent from it. And Paul’s arguments go deeper than boundary markers. The law fails because “through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20). He contrasts working for wages with believing (Romans 4:4–5), which is about doing anything at all, not just about badges of identity. He says Israel, “seeking to establish their own” righteousness, “did not submit to God’s righteousness” (Romans 10:3). And Paul’s own “righteousness of my own” included being “blameless” under the law (Philippians 3:6, 9). The boundary markers mattered precisely because they were part of a righteousness people thought they could stand on. As for “faith in Christ”, Paul settles the main point in the same verse by adding, “so we also have believed in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 2:16).

This commentary’s view: justification is God’s once-for-all legal declaration that the believing sinner is righteous, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness counted to him and received by faith alone; no one can merit anything. Works of the law include the Jewish boundary markers, as the New Perspective rightly sees, but Paul’s deeper question is how a sinner can be right with God, and his phrase means faith in Christ. The horizontal truth, one family of Jew and Gentile, grows out of the vertical one, the ungodly justified.

A Protestant woman and her Catholic neighbour read Romans 5 together over coffee for a year. They did not agree on everything. But one morning her neighbour said she had always expected to find out at the end whether she had done enough, and that “peace with God” sounded like something she wanted now.

For reflection

What does Roman Catholic teaching rightly guard, and why does it matter that renewal is the fruit and not the ground of justification? What has the New Perspective helped you see in Paul’s letters? How does justification by faith shape the way a church welcomes people from different backgrounds? How would you explain this chapter, kindly, to a Christian friend from another tradition?

8.title: Peace with God
8.essay:
Romans 5 begins with a “therefore”. Paul has spent four chapters explaining how the guilty are declared righteous. Now he tells us what the verdict does: “Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1).

The war is over

Peace with God is not first a feeling. It is a fact: the end of hostility between God and us. Paul is honest about what we were. Christ died “while we were still weak”, “while we were still sinners” and “while we were enemies” (Romans 5:6, 8, 10). He did not wait for us to improve, or to sue for peace. He made peace with his enemies at his own cost.

Then Paul reasons from the greater to the lesser: “Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God” (Romans 5:9). If God justified us when we were enemies, will he abandon us now that we are his friends? And the fruit of it is not only the absence of war but the presence of welcome: “Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand” (Romans 5:2). We stand. We do not crawl in each day hoping to be let in.

The courtroom empties

Romans 8 opens with the sentence every accused conscience longs to hear: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Then, near the end of the chapter, Paul brings us back into the courtroom one last time and invites any accuser to come forward. “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died” (Romans 8:33–34). The highest court has spoken, and the Judge is the one who acquits. The accuser has no case left to bring.

And we have an advocate: “if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). Notice his title. Our advocate does not plead that we are innocent. He pleads that he is righteous, and that he has already paid.

From the verdict, not for it

Here is the practical heart of the doctrine. Timothy Keller often pointed out that in every other approach to life, the performance leads to the verdict, while in the gospel the verdict comes before the performance. The justified believer has already heard the only verdict that finally matters. He lives from it, not for it.

That sets us free from the tyranny of performance. Our failures are real, and they grieve us, but they do not reopen the case. It also sets us free from the opinion of others. Paul could write, “But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself … It is the Lord who judges me” (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). When the Lord has already spoken, human courts, including the court of our own self-criticism, lose their power. The study The Fear of Man explores that freedom.

It makes honest confession possible. Luther described the believer as at the same time righteous and a sinner: righteous in Christ, still a sinner in himself. People who must defend their own record cannot afford to admit they were wrong. People whose record is Christ’s can. And it gives boldness in prayer: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). Charles Wesley caught the mood in his hymn “And Can It Be”: “No condemnation now I dread; Jesus, and all in him, is mine!”

A man who managed a busy team had never once, in twenty years, admitted a mistake at work. As he came to understand justification, something shifted. One Monday he stood up in a meeting and said that a costly decision had been his fault, and apologised. His team was stunned. He was not. He had nothing left to protect.

If guilt has become despair, and you have begun to think of ending your life, please do not wait: speak today to someone you trust, call your local emergency number or a crisis line, and let a pastor walk with you. The verdict of Romans 8:1 was spoken for people exactly like you.

My righteousness is in heaven

John Bunyan, the tinker who wrote The Pilgrim’s Progress, spent years tormented by fear that he was lost. In his autobiography, Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, he tells how one day, walking in a field, the words came into his mind: your righteousness is in heaven. He saw, with the eyes of faith, Jesus Christ at God’s right hand, and understood that his righteousness was not his good moods or his bad ones, but Christ himself, who is “the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8).

The LORD our righteousness

Six centuries before Christ, as Judah’s kings were failing and Jerusalem was about to fall, Jeremiah announced a coming King from David’s line, a righteous Branch. “And this is the name by which he will be called: ‘The LORD is our righteousness’” (Jeremiah 23:6). The king on the throne in Jeremiah’s later years was Zedekiah, whose own name was built from the same two words, “the LORD” and “righteousness”. He bore the name and betrayed it. The true King would not only bear it. He would be it.

Paul tells us who he is. Christ Jesus “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord’” (1 Corinthians 1:30–31). Job asked, “how can a man be in the right before God?” (Job 9:2). The full answer is not a doctrine, though it can be taught. It is not a feeling, though it brings deep peace. It is a name. When the accuser speaks, when conscience protests, when death comes near and the last court sits, the believer has one plea and needs no other: the LORD is my righteousness. And the Judge, who is also the Father, looks at the one who stands there clothed in his Son, and speaks over him the verdict he spoke over his Son at the empty tomb: righteous.

For reflection

What is the difference between living for a verdict and living from one? Whose opinion, including your own, has too much power over you, and how does 1 Corinthians 4:3–4 speak to it? What would honest confession look like for you this week? How does the name “The LORD is our righteousness” change the way you face your conscience, and your death?
